speaker: Edwin
content:
I'm teaching an undergraduate intro to computer science course next semester and
I need a simple website for it. What should be on it and how should I put it
together?

speaker: Claude
content:
## What belongs on it

An intro CS course site has one job: answer the questions students would otherwise email you. In rough priority order:

**Must have**
- **Header block** — course number/title, term, meeting times + room, your name, office hours (with location/Zoom link), TA names and hours.
- **Schedule table** — the single most-visited page. One row per class meeting: date, topic, readings, what's due. Keep assignment due dates *here* and nowhere else, so there's one source of truth.
- **Assignments** — link to specs/handouts, due dates, late policy, submission instructions.
- **Syllabus** — grading breakdown, collaboration/academic-integrity policy (spell out the AI-tool policy explicitly; in intro CS this is now the #1 source of disputes), accessibility statement, required software.
- **Getting started / setup** — how to install the language/toolchain on Mac, Windows, and Linux, plus a "it's broken" fallback (a browser-based option like Replit or a lab machine). Intro students lose the first two weeks to environment problems.

**Worth having**
- **Resources** — cheat sheets, recommended tutorials, past exams, tutoring center hours.
- **Getting help** — a decision tree: office hours vs. course forum vs. email, with expected response times. Saves you a lot of email.
- **FAQ** — grows each semester from actual student questions.

**Deliberately leave off**
Grades, anything FERPA-sensitive, and solutions — those go in the LMS (Canvas/Blackboard). Don't duplicate content between the site and the LMS; pick one home per item and link to it.

## How to build it

My recommendation: **Markdown files → a static site generator → GitHub Pages.** Free, no server to maintain, version-controlled (so next semester you branch last year's site and edit dates), and the schedule lives in a plain text file you can edit on your phone.

Concretely:

| Option | Good if |
|---|---|
| **GitHub Pages + Jekyll** (recommended) | You want zero setup — push Markdown, GitHub builds it. Theme like `just-the-docs` or `minima` gives you nav + search for free. |
| **Hugo or Quarto + GitHub Pages** | You want faster builds or to embed executable code/notebooks (Quarto is great for CS teaching material). |
| **A single hand-written `index.html`** | Genuinely fine if the site is one page. Don't over-engineer. |
| **Your university's CMS** | Only if IT requires it. |

Practical notes:
- **Put it under your own domain or a personal GitHub org**, not a per-semester repo buried in a department account — you'll reuse it.
- **Mobile-first.** Most students check the schedule on a phone between classes. Make sure the schedule table doesn't require horizontal scrolling.
- **Make it editable in under 60 seconds.** If updating a due date takes a build pipeline and a PR review, you'll stop doing it and the site will go stale — which is worse than no site.
- **Accessibility isn't optional** for a university site: real heading hierarchy, alt text, sufficient contrast, keyboard-navigable. Most default themes handle this; check with WAVE or Lighthouse.

## Want me to build it?

I can scaffold a working Jekyll site here — schedule table, assignments, syllabus, setup guide, all as Markdown with placeholder content you fill in — plus the GitHub Actions workflow to deploy it. Tell me the course name/number, the language you're teaching (Python? Java?), and the term, and I'll set it up.

speaker: Claude
content:
The single biggest risk in the first two weeks isn't the material — it's that your beginners conclude they're "not a computer person" before they've written anything. Almost every design decision below serves that one goal.

You have exactly **four meetings** in that window (Jan 13, 15, 20, 22), which is tight. Here's how I'd spend them.

## The core problem: a bimodal room

Some fraction of your students taught themselves Python in high school. They will answer questions fast, out loud, and correctly. Your beginners will read that as evidence about themselves rather than about prior exposure. This is the best-documented attrition mechanism in intro CS, and it operates in week one.

Practical countermeasures:

- **Name it on day one, explicitly.** "Some of you have programmed before. That's a head start, not a talent gap, and it disappears by midterm — that's not encouragement, it's what the grade distributions actually show." Beginners need to hear that the gap is expected and temporary.
- **Don't take hands for the first few classes.** Use think-pair-share or a polling tool instead. Cold-open hand-raising hands the floor to the experienced students and makes the gap the most visible thing in the room.
- **Give the experienced students somewhere to go.** An optional "extensions" section on each assignment absorbs their energy so it doesn't get spent dominating class.

## Separate "learning to program" from "fighting your laptop"

Setup failure is the most common way week one goes wrong, and it hits beginners hardest because they can't distinguish "Python isn't on my PATH" from "I don't understand programming."

**Do not require a local install before the first assignment.** Run weeks 1–2 entirely in a browser environment — Replit, or a Jupyter/Colab notebook — where every student is in an identical, working setup within 30 seconds. Then make **local installation its own scheduled lab** in week 3, with you and the TAs in the room, treated as a real topic rather than homework. Students who still can't get it working keep using the browser and lose nothing.

This alone is worth more to your beginners than any single lecture.

## Teach reading before writing

Beginners are usually pushed to author code before they can predict what code does, which means they're debugging a program and their own mental model simultaneously. Invert it for the first two weeks:

- **Trace, don't write.** Put five lines on the board, have them predict the output line by line, *then* run it. Every wrong prediction is a mental-model bug surfaced cheaply.
- **Use Python Tutor** (pythontutor.com) — it visualizes variables stepping forward. For "what is a variable, actually," it does in 90 seconds what a lecture does in 20 minutes.
- **Modify before authoring.** First exercises should be "here's working code, change it so it does X," not "write a program that does X." A blank editor is paralyzing; a working program with one thing to change is not.

## Make errors an explicit topic, not an interruption

Your beginners believe an error message means they broke something. Reframe it in week one: an error is the interpreter telling you where it got confused, and reading it is a skill with a procedure.

Teach the procedure: read the **last** line first, find the line number, look at *that* line and the one above it. Then deliberately break code in front of them — misspell a variable, drop a colon, mismatch a quote — and walk through each traceback. Making mistakes publicly and recovering calmly is the modeling that matters here.

## A concrete four-meeting plan

| Meeting | Focus |
|---|---|
| **Wed Jan 13** | Logistics, the bimodal-room talk, and a *live demo of something worth building*. End with everyone running `print("hello")` in the browser and seeing output. Everyone leaves having successfully executed code. |
| **Fri Jan 15** | Variables and types, taught by tracing. Python Tutor. Exercises are modify-this-code, not write-from-scratch. Emphasize: a variable is a labeled box, and `=` is not equality. |
| **Wed Jan 20** | Errors as a topic. Break code deliberately, read tracebacks together. Then expressions and `input()`/`print()`. **HW1 out.** |
| **Fri Jan 22** | Conditionals. Heavy pair work in class — you and TAs circulating. |

This shifts your current schedule slightly: conditionals still land Jan 22, but you've spent a half-meeting on errors and framing that the original plan gave to content. Worth it.

## Make HW1 nearly impossible to fail

HW1 (out Jan 20, due Jan 29) is where beginners form their self-assessment. Design it accordingly:

- **Very short** — 45 minutes for a beginner, 10 for someone experienced.
- **Mostly modify-and-extend**, one small write-from-scratch piece at the end.
- **Graded generously**, or credit/no-credit. Its job is proving "I can do this," not discriminating between students.
- **Include a required non-code question**: "What was the most confusing moment, and what did you do about it?" This surfaces where they're stuck and normalizes being stuck.
- **Due before the add/drop deadline** so their decision to stay is based on a real, successful experience.

## Two things to set up before day one

- **A day-one survey** (ungraded, not a pretest): prior experience, whether they have a working laptop, why they're taking the course. It tells you your actual bimodality and flags the students who'll need lab machines — before it becomes a problem.
- **A "help is normal" norm.** Tell them explicitly you expect them at office hours in the first two weeks, and that showing up without a specific question is fine. Beginners disproportionately believe office hours are for people who are already doing well.

---

One thing to be honest with yourself about: **four meetings is very little runway**, and Jan 12 being a Tuesday plus MLK Day is why. If you have any flexibility, the highest-value change is moving the local-install lab earlier and pushing conditionals to Jan 25 — that buys your beginners a full extra meeting before the first conceptual cliff, at the cost of one meeting's slack later in the term.
